newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Investors eye Kazakh privatisation with caution.
newsitem.headline: Investors eye Kazakh privatisation with caution.

text.p: Investors eyeing the vast mineral riches beneath Kazakhstan's wind-swept desert and steppe say they are put off by a privatisation programme as inhospitable as the territory.
Billions of dollars worth of oil, gas, metals and strategic industries make the former Soviet republic, five times the size of France, a potential gold mine for investors.
But accusations of corruption, murky deals and hazy laws have put off all but the most tenacious investors.
"There's a need for a set of rules that are open, transparent and fairly applied," said a Western diplomat.
He has had to listen time and again to complaints from businessmen from his home country on the haphazard nature of Kazakh privatisation.
The United States has offered the Kazakh government expertise from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to help stamp out corruption.
Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev vowed recently to change all that, demanding privatisation be wound up by the first half of 1998.
Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin, the man widely seen as the republic's main guarantor of market reforms, has promised clearer and more open rules for the tendering process.
SALE OF STATE ASSETS TO FILL COFFERS

But the Kazakh government, short of money to pay wages and pensions for the 16.9 million population, who have suffered a dramatic fall in living standards, is looking to a sell-off of state assets to fill its coffers and get the stalled economy back on its feet.

To get the ball rolling, the Kazakh capital Almaty's state-owned energy utility was sold to Belgium's Tractebel in August. Tractebel promised to invest $358 million in the run-down system while popping a further $340 million in the state treasury.
The large Yuzhneftegaz oil enterprise, with deposits totalling 581 million barrels of oil in central Kazakhstan, was sold to Canada's Hurricane Hydrocarbons Ltd for $120 million.

Hurricane promised to invest a further $280 million in the enterprise within six years and the Kazakh government is counting on over $2 billion in taxes and royalties from the deal over the next two decades.
The moving of energetic former central banker Grigory Marchenko to fire up the republic's sleepy securities market should also breathe life into Kazakh privatisation.
Marchenko said last month he aimed to kick-start the republic's dormant corporate market by preparing a set of "blue-chip" companies ready for trading by May 1997.

To this end, more oil enterprises, refineries, a gas pipeline network and the country's telecommunications are set to go under the hammer in the next few months. Bidders are expected to include big names like U.S. oil giant Texaco.
PROCESS TANGLED, INVESTORS CAUTIOUS
But despite efforts to quicken the tempo of privatisation, the process is still tangled and investor's doubts remain.
"We are not seeing as many foreign investors as we would like," said Yuzif Duberman, deputy chairman of Kazakhstan's privatisation committee.
Debts pose the main worry and were the subject of last-minute wrangling in the Yuzhneftegas deal.
Official sources say debts are holding up Deutsche Telekom's bid to buy a 49 percent stake in the state telecommunications monopoly, NAK Kazaktelekom.

"It's very difficult to find out the financial position of a company and what legal status it's in," said a Western lawyer based in Almaty. "For example, inflation makes the book value of debt different to its real value," he said.
Kazakh courts and regional officials have also been dragging their feet, afraid of bankruptcy measures and the effect tough managements will have on the already impoverished workforce.
"Around 80 to 90 percent of enterprises in Poland went through the bankruptcy process," said Asilkhan Dyusemgin, a Kazakh official charged with liquidating debt-ridden enterprises.

"But the courts don't want to liquidate enterprises as they are scared of answering for the consequences. It is also difficult with the akims (regional chiefs) who are against the bankruptcy process."
But a senior Western oil executive with long experience on frontier economies said he was prepared to wait it out.
"People tend to forget that this is all new for the Kazakhs," he said, "If you want to work in Kazakhstan, you've got to have patience."
